newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Charges hit British Gas earnings.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Charges hit British Gas earnings.

text.p: British Gas Plc on Thursday reported a sharp drop in earnings for the last year of its existence, hit by weak prices and restructuring charges.
The company, recently split up, said its historical cost profit on a pre-exceptional basis fell to 631 million pounds ($1.03 billion) in 1996 from 903 million a year earlier.
After exceptional items, the group's current cost result slipped to a loss of 571 million pounds versus a profit of 130 million in 1995.
"It's a year that's been dominated by big exceptional charges ... but the rest of the year's performance has been pretty good financially," said finance director Philip Hampton in an interview.

British Gas took exceptional charges of about 1.14 billion pounds in 1996, including 424 million for restructuring costs and charges of 635 million for the renegotiation of gas contracts and losses on long-term gas sales deals.
Earlier this month, British Gas demerged its gas supply business into a new company, Centrica Plc, and changed the name of its remaining gas transport and storage business to BG Plc.
BG had a proforma profit of 381 million pounds last year, while Centrica -- hit by gas contract charges -- posted a proforma loss of 1.06 billion pounds.
BG proposed a final dividend of 8.1 pence per share, making a total of 14.5 pence for the year.
Shares in BG rose 2-1/2 pence to 176, while Centrica shares firmed 1/4 pence to 68 at 1200 GMT, both in heavy trade.
British Gas said its earnings benefited from colder weather in 1996 but were hit by continuing weak prices in the industrial and commercial markets.
"The year opened with extremely low spot market prices but as we went through 1996, they rose quite sharply. But in recent weeks, they've fallen back again," Hampton said.
"I think they'll continue to be fairly volatile," he added.

BG still faced uncertainty over an enquiry into a tough pricing policy proposed by regulators but Hampton said the company continued to believe the review by the Monopolies and Mergers Commission (MMC) would be published in April.

The matter was passed to the MMC for a ruling after British Gas contested a recommendation by industry regulator Ofgas for strict price controls on what BG could charge gas suppliers for transporting their gas.
"We have no firm indication that there's any reason for advancement or delay. We're still working on the assumption that it will hit its timetable," Hampton said.

There has been vague market speculation that the review might be delayed until after British elections, due by May, thus prolonging uncertainty about the impact of the Ofgas proposals on BG's profits.
In other matters, Hampton said the company had not seen any dramatic changes in market share at a pilot project which introduced domestic competition in southwest England.

"Clearly, there is a lot of brand loyalty to British Gas but it's too early to judge how the loyalty is going to be sustained," he said, adding that the firm had improved service to help keep market share.
"We've been improving our service standards in a measurable way quite significantly but we still have some way to go," Hampton said. ($1=.6109 Pound)
